analytic.title: An Algorithm for Scheduling Aperiodic Real-time Tasks on a Static Schedule

div.p: In many real-time systems, there are not only periodic real-time tasks, but also aperiodic real-time tasks arising from arbitrary critical events. In this paper, we propose an algorithm (SATSS , Schedule Aperiodic Tasks on a Static Schedule) scheduling both periodic real-time tasks and aperiodic real-time tasks. This algorithm first produces a schedule which consists of only periodic tasks before the system is started and schedules aperiodic tasks on the static schedule on run time. It can guarantee all accepted tasks' deadlines by testing the schedulability of aperiodic tasks in a busy period consisting of not only the running tasks but also the periodic tasks in future. Experimental results show that the algorithm is effective.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time systems are defined as those systems in which the correctness of the system depends not only on the logical result of computation, but also on the time at which the results are produced [1]. Real-time systems can be broadly classified into three categories: hard real-time systems, firm real-time systems and soft realtime systems [2]. Typical examples of hard real-time systems are avionic control and nuclear plant control. In these systems, periodic and aperiodic tasks co-exist. The periodic tasks typically arise from sensor data or control loops, while the aperiodic tasks generally arise from operator actions or arbitrary events.

Scheduling both periodic and aperiodic tasks in realtime systems is more difficult than scheduling periodic or aperiodic tasks alone. The simplest method is to treat the aperiodic tasks as background tasks when their response times are not critical. The common method is to create a periodic server for servicing aperiodic tasks within the computation time that is allocated to the server, such as the polling server, the deferrable server, and the priority exchange algorithms [3,4]. The average response time of aperiodic tasks is improved through the use of a server. The slack stealing (SS) algorithm [5] creates a passive task to service aperiodic tasks by stealing all the available processing time from periodic tasks. SS is optimal in the sense that all available processing time will be exploited for servicing aperiodic tasks. However, in order to exploit all processing time left by a given set of periodic tasks, SS uses a trial and error method to find the solution iteratively, thus a significant amount of time is needed to find an optimal solution. In [6], a reservation based (RB) algorithm is proposed for uniprocessor systems. RB reserves a fraction of processor time for executing aperiodic tasks. It may allocate the same amount of processing time as SS to service aperiodic tasks by deriving the least upper bound of reserved processor time in some cases. In [7], a hybrid scheduling scheme for hard, soft and non-realtime tasks is proposed. The scheme creates a constant utilization server for each real-time scheduling policy and a total bandwidth server for all the non-real-time tasks with time sharing scheduling policy. Each server has a scheduler, called server scheduler, which is responsible for executing the ready-to-run tasks with the same scheduling policy as the server. All the servers are scheduled by the bottom operating system scheduler according to EDF algorithm. Hybrid scheduling algorithm in [8] can schedule time triggered tasks and event triggered tasks. The two schemes in [7] and [8] are similar, i.e. their schedulers are hierarchical. The top schedulers schedule tasks with the same scheduling policy and the bottom scheduler allocates computing time for each top schedulers.

If we have no knowledge about arrival times and frequencies of aperiodic tasks, it is very difficult to determine a period and computation time of a periodic server for servicing aperiodic tasks. In this paper, we propose an algorithm that doesn't need a server and it guarantee all accepted tasks' deadlines by testing the schedulability of tasks in a busy period.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 addresses the problem. In section 3 we introduce a dynamic schedulability criterion and algorithm for scheduling aperiodic tasks on a static schedule. In section 4, simulation experiments are provided to show the algorithm's effectiveness. Finally, we make our concluding remarks in Section 5.

div.head: II. PROBLEM DESCRIPTION AND TASK MODEL
div.p: The schedulability of periodic tasks whose characteristics are known a priori is guaranteed because they are scheduled statically before the system is started. Our goal is guaranteeing the schedulability of aperiodic tasks on a static schedule which consist of periodic tasks only. To simplify the problem, we assume that all tasks are independent. It means that tasks have no precedence constraints. Generally, tasks with precedence constraints can be scheduled by transforming the precedence graph into independent nodes with new ready times and deadlines [9].

A real-time periodic task system consists of a set of n periodic tasks τ = {τ 1 , τ 2 … τ n }. Each task τ i must be executed once every T i time units, where T i is the period of τ i . Each execution of a periodic task is called a job (or request), and every job of τ i has a computation (or execution) time e i . The jth job of τ i is denoted as τ ij for all 1≤i≤n and j≥1. τ ij is ready for execution at time (j-1)×T i and must be completed by the start time of the next job period of the same task, which is equal to j×T i . We define r ij = (j-1)×T i to be the release time (or request time) and d ij = j×T i the deadline of τ ij . The finish time f ij of τ ij is determined by schedule algorithm. For simplicity, we denote a periodic task τ i as τ i (T i , e i ).

div.head: III. SCHEDULING APERIODIC TASKS
div.p: In this section, we discuss the problem of scheduling real-time aperiodic tasks on a static schedule which consists of only periodic tasks. Firstly, some concepts and definitions are given. Then the schedulability of aperiodic tasks is analyzed. Finally, a scheduling algorithm is proposed that can schedule task set consist of both periodic tasks and aperiodic tasks.

div.head: A. Schedulability analysis
div.p: Definition 1 (Busy Period) A busy period is a time interval [s, t] that satisfies the following 3 constraints:
1) All requests made before s are completed by s;
2) All requests made before t are completed by t;
3) For every u ∈ (s, t), there exists at least one request arrived before u, and is not completed by u.
In other words, at least one task is running in a busy period.

Definition 2 (Executing Task and Reserved Task) Suppose that the current time is ct. An executing task δ i is a task whose release time r i <ct and hasn't fulfilled yet; A reserved task δ i is a task which is schedulable and its release time r i is determined but r i >ct, for example a job of a periodic task.

Because between two adjacent busy periods there is a gap in which the processor is idle, the task set in one busy period has no influence on the schedulability of task set in the other busy period. To guarantee all tasks' deadlines, we only need to test the schedulability of aperiodic tasks in a busy period including reserved periodic tasks.

div.head: B. SATSS scheduling algorithm
div.p: Scheduling aperiodic tasks on a static schedule needs to test the tasks' schedulability in a busy period and the number of the tasks maybe very large [11] when the periodic tasks' utilization is close to 100%. If the number of tasks to be tested is large, the schedule overhead is high. To reduce the schedule overhead, another schedule scheme is provided: virtual task scheme and we call the original scheme as single task scheme. We define a virtual task as a task that consists of all tasks in a busy period [s, t] which are composed of periodic tasks only and its release time r = s, executing time e = t -s that is the length of the busy period, deadline d = t + min (δ i .d i -δ i .f i ) for every task δ i in the busy period [s, t]. According to virtual task scheme, a virtual task is one schedule unit which may consist of many tasks and the schedule overhead reduce greatly.

When virtual task scheme is used, the periodic tasks set can be scheduled with any schedule algorithm such as RM, EDF and so on and when a virtual task is ready to execute, tasks consisting the virtual task must be scheduled with corresponding schedule algorithm. div.head: IV. SIMULATION RESULTS
div.p: The SATSS algorithm is intended for use in scheduling both periodic and aperiodic real-time tasks to meet their deadlines. In order to show its advantages and limits, we analyze and compare the SATSS algorithm against the classic methods such as the SS [5] and RB [6].

We first generate a set of N periodic real-time tasks. For i≤N, the task's period T i is uniformly distributed in [100, 500] and execution time C i is in [0, ηT i ]. We use N and η to control the periodic tasks' load. Then we generate a set of K aperiodic real-time tasks and they arrive as an independent Poisson process with parameter λ. For k≤K, the task's relative deadline D k is uniformly distributed in [100, 500] and execution time C k is in [0, σD k ]. λ and σ are used to control the aperiodic tasks' load. We define the reject ratio as the ratio of the number of rejected aperiodic tasks to the total number of aperiodic tasks arrived. Four sets of experiments are conducted to evaluate the performance of the SATSS algorithm. The first set of experiments is performed with respect to the influence of different periodic task load on the reject ratio of aperiodic tasks. By changing the value N (1≤N≤10) and η (0<η≤0.1), various sets of periodic tasks are generated with different load. We test the aperiodic tasks reject ratio with parameters σ=0.1 and λ=0.03 and their load is about 0.5. The experimental results are shown in figure 3.

The second set of experiments is performed with respect to the influence of aperiodic task's frequencies on the reject ratio. We first schedule a set of periodic tasks with N=10 and η=0.1 and their load is about 0.5. By changing the value λ (0.01≤λ≤0.03), various sets of aperiodic tasks are generated with parameter σ=0.1. We test the reject ratio with different value of λ. The experimental results are shown in figure 4.

From above 2 figures, we can see that with the task load increase, the reject ratio also increase for three algorithms and the reject ratio of SATSS is always lower than the other two. Scheduling aperiodic tasks on a static schedule needs to test the schedulability not only of the executing tasks but also of the reserved tasks in a busy period and the conversional EDF algorithm only needs to test the executing tasks. We define the average ratio of reserved tasks number to executing tasks number in a busy period as extra overhead. The third set of experiments is performed with respect to the extra overhead under different periodic task load. In the experiments, the periodic task set and aperiodic task set are the same as the first set of experiments. The forth set of experiments is performed with respect to the extra overhead under different aperiodic task's frequencies. In these experiments, the periodic task set and aperiodic task set are the same as the second set of experiments. Their results are shown in figure 5 and figure 6 respectively.

From the results we can see that the extra overhead according to the virtual task scheme (VTS) is lower than that according to single task scheme (STS). We also can see that with task load increase, the extra overhead of single task scheme also increase and the extra overhead of virtual task scheme keeps the same on the whole.

div.head: V. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In this paper, we propose a real-time scheduling algorithm which can schedule both periodic tasks and aperiodic tasks. The algorithm schedules the periodic tasks firstly before the system is started and schedules the aperiodic tasks dynamically on the schedule produced by the periodic tasks. By testing the schedulability of tasks in a busy period including periodic tasks in future, the algorithm make all accepted tasks meet their deadline. The experimental results demonstrate that the algorithm has advantages over the SS algorithm and RB algorithm in terms of task reject ratio.
